questions.question: Define weathering, erosion and deposition and explain how they form a chain.
questions.expected_answer: Weathering: breakdown of rock in place at/near the surface (physical, chemical, biological). Erosion: wearing away, removal and transport of material by agents (running water, wind, ice, waves, gravity). Deposition: laying down of transported material when the agent loses energy. Chain: weathering prepares loose material, erosion moves it (more easily once weathered), deposition builds landforms and sediments that may become sedimentary rock ("breaks, takes, drops"); denudation = weathering + erosion.

questions.question: Describe the agents of erosion and how rivers and wind erode and transport material.
questions.expected_answer: Running water (main agent in SA): rain splash, sheet wash, rills, dongas; river erosion by hydraulic action, abrasion/corrasion, attrition, solution; transport by traction, saltation, suspension, solution. Wind: deflation and abrasion in dry, bare areas (Kalahari, Namib); saltation and suspension of dust. Ice: glaciers pluck and scrape (Dwyka tillite about 300 million years ago). Waves: coastal erosion and beaches. Gravity: mass movement - rockfalls, landslides, mudflows, soil creep.

questions.question: Explain why deposition occurs and use a South African example to show weathering, erosion and deposition working together.
questions.expected_answer: Deposition occurs when agents lose energy (river slows on bends, flat land, at mouths; wind slows behind obstacles); largest material dropped first (sorting). Example: diamonds in kimberlite pipes near Kimberley weathered and eroded; Orange River transported them to the Atlantic; deposited in river gravels and, moved by waves, on Namaqualand/Namibian beaches. Or Drakensberg basalt frost-weathered, carried by rivers such as the Tugela and deposited on flood plains and at the coast; siltation of dams.
